title: Net assets that move with no line to explain them
question: Does each return add up: opening net assets, plus the year's surplus or deficit, plus the other changes the return itself lists, equal to closing net assets?
finding: Of 2,343 returns tested, 16 from 9 organizations leave $25,000 or more (and at least 1% of the year's spending) unexplained, $10.6 million in all. The largest is St James Infirmary: net assets of $5.9 million at the start of the year ended 30 June 2024, a reported surplus of $68,843, and $204,560 at the end, leaving $5.8 million with no entry. In 7 of the 16 the net-asset lines are simply blank or zero, which points to an incomplete form.
how: From each return: net assets at the start and end of the year, revenue less expenses, and the five lines on which a return reports other changes in net assets (unrealised investment gains, donated services, investment expenses, prior-period adjustments, other changes). Closing net assets are compared with opening plus all of those. Preparers enter donated services and investment expenses inconsistently, so the sum is tried with and without the first and with either sign of the second, and the smallest difference is kept. Listed when the difference is at least $25,000 and 1% of expenses. A negative figure means net assets are lower than the lines explain.
limits: A return is prepared from the books but is not the books. A figure typed on the wrong line, a balance left blank, or an adjustment made in the accounts and not carried to the form produces a difference with no money missing; where the next year shows an equal and opposite difference, that is the likely cause. An organization that is closing may hand its assets to a successor and should say so on the return. Only the audited statements, or the workpapers, can say which. A gap is a reason to ask for the audited statements, not a finding.
